analysis.one_liner: Requires employer health plans to cover mental health and addiction treatment on equal terms with medical care.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 255 House cosponsors—a majority of the chamber—yet never received a vote, sitting in three committees until the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required group health plans—those offered through employers—to stop treating mental health and substance-use care worse than physical care. If a plan did not impose visit limits, day caps, higher copays, or separate deductibles on ordinary medical care, it could not impose them on mental health or addiction treatment. It also would have required plans that offer any mental health coverage to cover the same conditions covered by the most popular federal employee plan, and to disclose the reasons for denying care. It never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of workers and families with employer-sponsored insurance who need mental health or substance-use treatment. Today, plans routinely cap therapy visits and inpatient days and charge higher copays for psychiatric care than for other care; this bill would have outlawed those unequal limits and cost-sharing, required disclosure of medical-necessity criteria and denial reasons, and expanded the definition of covered conditions to include substance-use disorders.

how_it_helps.text: Bars plans from imposing treatment limits—caps on visits or days of coverage—on mental health and substance-use benefits unless the same or an equally common limit applies to medical and surgical benefits in the same category (inpatient or outpatient, in or out of network).

Bars plans from imposing higher deductibles, copays, or coinsurance on mental health and substance-use benefits than the predominant cost-sharing applied to medical and surgical benefits in the same category.
Extends existing parity rules to substance-use disorder benefits, which prior law expressly excluded, and removes the sunset date so the parity requirement does not expire.

Requires plans that offer any mental health or addiction benefits to cover every condition covered by the federal employee health plan option with the highest enrollment, a floor for the scope of coverage.
Requires plan administrators to disclose their medical-necessity criteria on request and to give patients the reason for any denial of mental health or addiction treatment payment.

Provides a cost escape valve: a plan whose total costs rise more than 2 percent the first year (1 percent in later years) because of the new rules can be exempt for one plan year, certified by a qualified actuary.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor group health plans and their insurers bear the cost of equalizing mental health and addiction coverage, which would be passed to employers and, through premiums, to workers generally. Insurers lose flexibility to manage mental health benefits more restrictively than other care.

drawbacks.text: Equalizing mental health coverage raises plan costs. The bill's own cost exemption—letting plans off the rules for a year if costs rise more than a set percentage—acknowledges this, but it also means plans that clear the threshold can drop the protections for a year.
The mandate does not apply to small employers with 50 or fewer employees, leaving workers at small firms without the protection.

Plans are not required to offer mental health benefits at all; the rules bind only plans that choose to provide some mental health or addiction coverage, so a plan could avoid the mandate by dropping those benefits.
The bill explicitly does not touch the federal law that limits state-level remedies for self-insured employer plans, so enforcement avenues for workers remain limited.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit—ending second-class coverage for mental illness and addiction, conditions that affect a large share of working families—is substantial and directly targets a practice that shifts costs onto the sickest patients. The costs are real but bounded: studies cited in the parity debate generally found parity could be done for low single-digit premium increases, and the bill builds in an actuary-certified exemption for plans facing higher cost increases. The main design weakness is the small-employer exemption and the possibility that some plans drop mental health benefits to escape the mandate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and bounced among their subcommittees all year, was never reported out, and died without a floor vote when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Patrick Kennedy (D-RI) introduced the bill on March 7, 2007, joined by an initial list of cosponsors that included Republicans such as Rep. Jim Ramstad.
The Speaker referred it to three committees—Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means—so any of them had to act before it could move.
Within weeks it was further referred to subcommittees (March 8, March 16, and June 5, 2007), where it sat.
No committee ever reported the bill, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the record shows no action after the June 2007 subcommittee referral for the rest of the two-year Congress.
The bill ended the Congress with 255 cosponsors, including 222 Democrats and 33 Republicans—a majority of the House—without ever receiving a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employer health plans and insurers were better off in the short run because they avoided the House bill's stricter parity requirements, which went further than the Senate version by extending parity to substance-use treatment and adding disclosure rules. A close relative of the proposal did become law later in 2008 (the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act), softening the eventual loss for the industry.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employer health plans and insurers, at least until a later version passed

against.what_they_did: Lobbied against the House bill's stricter parity provisions, citing premium cost increases for employers.

sides.party_line_note: Support was strongly bipartisan on paper: 222 of 255 cosponsors were Democrats but 33 were Republicans, and the bill was co-introduced by a Republican, Jim Ramstad; there was never a roll call, so no party split ever showed up in a vote.

industries.industry: Health insurers and group health plan administrators
industries.note: The bill would have forced them to equalize mental health and addiction coverage and to disclose medical-necessity criteria and denial reasons, ending a practice of capping and cost-shifting psychiatric care. Those restrictions cost the industry money that would otherwise come from patients' pockets.

Employers would have borne higher premiums for richer mental health coverage, though the bill included an actuary-certified exemption letting plans off for a year if costs rose more than the allowed percentage. Small employers with 50 or fewer workers were exempt entirely.

industries.industry: Mental health and addiction treatment providers
industries.note: Ending visit caps, day limits, and higher copays would have opened a much larger pool of insured patients able to afford therapy, inpatient care, and substance-use treatment.
